Every adult in this film operates with the same scripted obliviousness - a village full of people who cannot hear a child asking a simple question, not because the film has something to say about how the world ignores children, but because the plot requires him to keep running. The frustration isn't the productive kind that builds toward meaning; it's the mechanical kind where you can see the hand of the script redirecting every conversation away from resolution, and by the halfway mark the contrivance has drained whatever warmth the premise held. Kiarostami would go on to make Taste of Cherry, a film that earns its circling - this one just circles.

Maybe I woke up on the wrong side of the bed this morning, I’ve been struggling as of late and this particular morning was especially heavy in some respects, but I was much less into this movie than I expected to be. In fact… It kinda did the opposite of give me hope? It’s rad that other people at Film School took Where Is The Friend’s House? as an exercise in compassion and humanity’s good, but uh… Woof. Every single adult in this made me so angry. They were so cruel and uncaring that it was hard for me to think that any of the kids who were so kind hearted here would ever grow up in a society where they could hold on to that goodness. It’s certainly impactful in its exploration of kids being much more compassionate than adults, but you pair what I took as a rather negative view of what the world does to people over time with the incredibly rhythmic (dare I say repetitive) structure and I couldn’t help but be left frustrated by this film. Maybe this is more so because I am so frustrated by the way life itself is going, however? There was some humor that I’ll admit vibed with me and the main character’s sweetness is undeniably wholesome at times, but the bleak portrayal of the adults and world around our protagonist constantly kept me in a state of discomfort. I was feeling a whole lot of dread for my own future as someone who has been desperately fighting to cling on to the hope I had as a kid. Where Is The Friend’s House? is an interesting movie that I think is well made on the whole but it just didn’t quite jive for me personally. In a weird way I guess I think it’s good, but still don’t really like it? I dunno. I feel guilty for not loving it but I did still end up having a great time chatting with folks at Film School about it after our screening. The night’s conversations definitely made me reflect on the movie in ways that made it much more compelling to me in retrospect. The drive to Portland was still very much worth it for that camaraderie too. It feels really good to be a part of a community and that was one of the things I was really worried about missing out on in life when I woke up this morning. So, at the end of the night my spirits were lifted a bit after all thanks to being among a room of friends who love my favorite art form as much as me and continually open my eyes to new ways of understanding film. Boy is this life hard though… Maybe I’ll have to revisit Where Is The Friend’s House? when mine is in a more stable place. Or at least a more hopeful one? Life can be a lot of things, but I’m not sure if stable will ever be one of them.

I think I understood what this film was trying to say very early on, and I don't think the journey from that point on till that beautiful last shot was really earned for me. There were excruciatingly long scenes of the boy Ahmed repeating the same sentence about 40 different times, and whether it was his mother, or his grandpa, or some random people in Poshteh, would just respond with their own sentence 40 times as well. I made the mistake of watching Yi Yi before this, and Yi Yi was a film where 3 hours felt like 2. In this film, 83 minutes felt like 183 minutes. Every scene felt unbearably repetitive, with not even the bare minimum happening to progress the story or dive deeper into the themes. It was only when Ahmad met the old doormaker that I actually found myself being immersed in the film and the characters. The old doormaker was by far the most interesting and fascinating character in this film, and there seemed to be more depth for Ahmad once he had more than one line to say. The final shot is beautiful, it reminds me very much of A Moment Of Innocence . But I don't think the 'innocence' and empathy of this film is earned as much as it is in Makhmalbaf's film. I understood this film after the first 15 minutes, and the rest of the 70 minutes, much like Ahmad's own journey, felt like a formality to lead me to somewhere I already was. I love Iranian cinema, I love docu-drama cinema, and I love Kiarostami. But this was such a frustrating film to sit through. The characters felt way too one-dimensional, and frustratingly simplistic, like cardboard cutouts. You can't make a character repeat the same line 483 different times within 83 minutes and not expect people to grow sick of it.

Ce que cherche à faire Kiarostami apparaît assez clairement dès lors qu’on accepte de se tenir dans la durée qu’il impose, puisque tout son geste consiste à prendre une situation d’une simplicité nue et à la pousser jusqu’à un point où celle-ci devient presque intenable : un enfant qui veut simplement faire ce qui lui semble juste, se heurtant à un monde adulte qui n’oppose pas une méchanceté spectaculaire mais une forme d’inertie opaque faite d’habitudes, d’autorité automatique et d’une incapacité fondamentale à reconnaître la vérité pourtant immédiate de ce qui est dit. La répétition devient le cœur même du dispositif de ce film, de sorte que le spectateur se trouve progressivement pris dans une temporalité qui ne lui offre aucune échappée, chaque tentative de l’enfant reconduisant à la même incompréhension, et alors notre agacement se fait de plus en plus pressant. Le film dit sans doute quelque chose également de l’incapacité des gens, à fortiori des adultes, à se comprendre, car même dans les scènes de dialogue entre adultes uniquement, il y a beaucoup de tension et de mauvaises compréhensions, malgré que tous se répètent. C’est à cet endroit que la dimension la plus forte du film se laisse saisir, dans cette contradiction entre une exigence abstraite portée par l’école, avec une modernisation et une tentative de démocratisation de l’éducation à cette période de l’histoire initiée par l’État, et les contraintes concrètes de la vie de la paysannerie, deux visions qui se retrouvent matériellement en contradiction. Celles-ci viennent sans cesse redistribuer les priorités de sorte que l’enfant ne peut jamais coïncider avec ce qu’on attend de lui, pris dans une injonction double dont il ne peut sortir qu’en étant fautif. Que le film produise de l’ennui ou de l’irritation n’a alors rien d’étonnant. Si la scène finale ouvre bien un moment d’émotion elle ne suffit pas nécessairement à transformer l’expérience en plaisir. Tout ça pour dire que je reconnaît la cohérence voire la force du film, mais je ne l’ai pas aimé, j’ai eu le sentiment d’avoir été retenu dans quelque chose qui ne me correspond pas. Autrement dit, j’ai vu d’autres films dont le thème principal était la domination adulte qui, en étant fins eux aussi, et bien que m’ayant rendu très triste, m’ont fait passer un meilleur moment.

Where Is the Friend’s House? is a film with some genuinely wonderful qualities, but personally, I just couldn’t fully connect with it. What bothered me most was the way the adults are portrayed. Ahmad desperately walks around the village trying to return his friend Mohammad Reza Nematzadeh’s notebook, yet one adult after another fails to properly listen to what he is saying. I understand that the film is trying to explore the idea that “adults don’t understand children,” but it often feels like the characters are deliberately written to make the audience side with Ahmad and become frustrated with the adults. There are several scenes where a child is desperately trying to explain his situation, only for the adult to keep talking about something completely unrelated. At times, it felt a little too obvious that the film was trying to make me go, “Oh my god, just LISTEN to the kid.” Of course, the adults aren’t all portrayed as simply bad people. Even the teacher has his reasons: Mohammad Reza Nematzadeh has repeatedly ignored the same rule, and toward the end he even tells the other students that people should be allowed a few mistakes. That makes it difficult to reduce the adults to a simple good-versus-evil dynamic. Still, the film’s structure clearly seems designed to push the audience emotionally toward Ahmad. In that respect, I think François Truffaut’s The 400 Blows, which deals with the same basic idea of “adults don’t understand children,” handles it much better. The adults there have their own reasons and circumstances, while the protagonist himself is far from blameless. Yet we still sympathize with him because nobody really understands him, leaving us with much more complicated feelings. That said, there are definitely things I loved about Where Is the Friend’s House? The music that plays when Ahmad decides to return the notebook and sets off on his journey is absolutely beautiful. It makes this simple errand feel like a genuinely huge adventure from a child’s perspective. I also loved the way the flower is used throughout the film. The flower Ahmad receives from the craftsman, and especially the flower placed inside the notebook at the end, is a beautiful touch. It quietly symbolizes what Ahmad did for his friend and gives the ending a lovely sense of aftertaste. I’m very drawn to Kiarostami’s cinematic sensibility and the beauty of his filmmaking, and I certainly don’t think this is a bad movie. I just found the way it portrays the relationship between children and adults somewhat too deliberate and manipulative for my taste. I still prefer Taste of Cherry, which I watched previously, especially for its ambiguity and the distance it maintains between its characters. This is only the first film of the trilogy, and I still haven’t seen the other two, so I definitely don’t want to judge the entire Koker trilogy based on this one movie. I’m 100% watching all three though. Can’t leave it at just one lol.

Doesn’t exactly paint parents or adults in a flattering light.  Maybe it’s exaggerated, but I definitely remember adults seeming dismissive to the point of exasperation as a kid.  I probably had the benefit of being able to speak up without much consequence.  The adults here seem especially strict, and uninterested in actually hearing him. The film has a beautiful understanding of a well-meaning child’s perspective.  Ahmad’s mission is enormously important to him, and Kiarostami makes it just as important to us.

Çünki başqalarının məni yıxıldığım üçün tənqid edəcəyini, zəif görəcəyini düşünmüşəm. Məni qaldıran bir dostum olmayıb. Bəlkə də buna görə filmdəki o balaca uşağın digər uşağa göstərdiyi qayğı mənə bu qədər toxundu. Sonra evdə ana ilə uşağın münasibəti göstərilir və yenə özümü gördüm. A true hero's journey. A story that appears to be about a boy simply returning his friend's school notebook reveals itself as heartwarming experience about doing the right thing in the face of adversity. I have seen a lot of conversations where people emphasize that this story is about childhood innocence, or that it's about being a good friend. I agree with those things, but what I don't see talked about enough is how this works as an analog for maintaining one's morals despite persecution. Yes, it is wonderful to see a young boy who is so willing to help his friend, but he is also doing so while facing relatively massive difficulties. While asking his mother if he could return his friend's notebook he accidentally took, she repeatedly ignores him. When she does finally listen to him, she doesn't believe him. Then she tasks him with taking care of his baby brother, or bringing her the wash basin as she's doing laundry. This boy isn't even able to sit and do his own homework uninterrupted, let alone get time to help his friend. It's only when he receives another chore to bring home some bread is he able to slip out, surely well aware of the punishment he will receive when he returns, to attempt to find his friend and return his notebook. We know this is just a strict parent, but this and other experiences with adults as the film goes along gives us a strong theme of staying true to your morals and operating under authoritarianism. Nearly every adult the boy interacts with is makes his journey more difficult. The mother is unreasonable, the iron door salesman is dishonest, and the grandfather is borders on sadistic in regard to his philosophy on discipline. Even with the massive consequences at stake (at least in the eyes of an 8 year old boy), he tirelessly pursues every lead he can to find his friend. He's not only good friend because he wants to return the book, he's good because of wanting to do the right thing even when he is at odds with authority and faces punishment. What the film does best is actualizing the stakes of life as a child. Even watching this as an adult, the film makes this boy's day of trouble feel like a world ending event. I've seen many who recommended this as a film for children, and while I agree, I think it would have a more profound impact on adults. A child may takeaway that you should always try to do the right thing and help your friends, but an adult watching this and learning to empathize with the "small" struggles of children would honestly make them better parents and kinder people as a whole. It's a lovely and morally sound film.

Grandfather's Friend: What I mean to say is, suppose the kid did nothing wrong. What would you do? What then? Grandfather: I'd find an excuse and give him a beating every other week. So he wouldn't forget. As my debut watch of an Abbas Kiarostami film, my expectations were extremely high for the first installment of the Koker trilogy, but boy was I blown away. Let's start to quickly say that the quote I selected to represent the film is for me not the most memorable, or may not portray the majority of what the film is based around, but it is for me the most pivotal moment of the film, giving the audience the truth as to the brutality of fear. Fear constantly lingers in the life of Ahmed's life, watching his classmate Mohamed getting berated for forgetting his notebook, leading to a threat from the class teacher of being expelled if the defiance continued. For obvious reason of the major threat being issued for a minor problem, Mohamed begins to cry, and when the teacher tells Mohamed to look back up to him, the camera cuts to Ahmed, who also listens to him out of reluctance, who's eyes look from the ground to the teacher's eyes. There should be authority in a class-room, there should be the difference between right or wrong clearly understood for all the students to learn, but to abuse the power given and cast the children you teach under an apprehensive spell feels wrong, making this film feel like a critique of Iran's education system, even though this probably isn't why everyone likes this film. Kiarostami is quick to show the mundane of Ahmed's life, the chores, the homework, and the reluctance from his mother to listen to him. He shows how Ahmed, despite his age, has some form of intelligence he carries, and persistently repeats the same dialogue in an attempt to convince his mother to travel from Koker to Poshteh through a zig-zagging path on a hill. Kiarostami shows the dehumanising neglect that affects Ahmed's life within and outside the school facility, and the other children, to work for their parents and constantly provide in need and support when asked for, which is a struggle for the teacher to instruct them to balance, with this being a constant theme that's bought up throughout. Yet, this shows the stereotypical dynamic of the mother's role in society, with her dirty, white clothing matching the washing that surrounds her, which shows at times she is without a purpose or a voice, someone to blend with the surroundings and do their job annually, without going further, making change or taking a different step, due to fear or potentially the way the patriarchal society sets up the woman's role. The inability to be capable of an identity can perhaps be interpreted as reflecting the political and social pressures of post-revolutionary Iran. Although I would not claim that Kiarostami is directly allegorising the Iranian regime, the restrictions placed upon Ahmed's freedom, both in and out the classroom made me wonder how authority can suppress individuality, creating an overwhelming culture surrounding Iran consistent of fear. This can all be interpreted from the first fifteen minutes, with long-duration, static shots used to show the mundane dullness of Ahmed's personal life, and the errands he runs, with the atmosphere of the white walls representing how the people can't escape the control enforced on them, and feels indoctrinated and forced to accept the radical changes surrounding them. The quote I highlighted was the first and only one I found on IMDB, but it resonated with me as to the meaning of this film as a critique of Iran's political state, but when I watched it, and the grand-father explaining how he was beat or given a penny weekly, regardless on his good behaviour, it shows the punishment descending beyond their own eyes. That in an inability to realise the transition that beatings without a motive is just cruel, and adds further fear on the children, shows that the grandfather may not fully accept what happened in his childhood, that the beatings he took didn't make him as a person, it would make some rebel. I guess Kiarostami may use this reflective conversation that abrupts the tight-pace the film uses when progressing through Ahmed's odyssey as a form of escapism to tell the audience metaphorically the message of the film, that the cycle of abuse does not shape how a person grows up for the better, and there needs to be a change that can enhance stability, perhaps further going against the Iranian regime with this. (This is all speculation, it's what I interpret after a first watch, but of course I could be wrong with all this.) A really cool use of cinematography and blocking is further used half-way when Ahmed reaches a child that has the same last name as Mohamed, but isn't him, and Kiarostami hides this through using him carrying a heavy box on his shoulders to cover his identity, in a genius way to add mystery and suspense. From the point-of-view shot, although the audience is certain that it won't be Mohamed, there is still speculation and possibility as to the identity of Mohamed. This further is a metaphor to the role of the teacher, that the mask they put on to try and help the children learn may not be who they really are, two different sides of the person, and that although in the beginning sequence the teacher may try to have order and rules within his classroom, the way he goes about the good intentions is wrong, so disappoints us like the reveal of the boy's identity, and makes a child cry. There are some really nice shots in this, of Ahmed running through the woods, of Ahmed walking up the hill to get to Poshteh, and the direction that Kiarostami takes you on in the journey is really genius, I love Kiarostami already from this. To be honest, the pacing did drag slightly, but now I write this review, it didn't at all, for I was confused as to the old man that takes Ahmed to a house, and what his purpose was, but it makes complete sense. The caring nature sparks a difference in Ahmed's life, who offers to help him and attempt to be kind, but by this time Ahmed is not entertained, rebelling and asking him to walk faster despite a clear lack of mobility due to age presumably, which Ahmed is oblivious to. Abkar (the old man) represents to us what Kiarostami would fantasise a perfect Iran would be portrayed as, with peace and innocence, yet the fragility is shown clearly through the wholes in his socks in his poverty-stricken house, where the red marks on his heel of his feet represent two things. One: there has to be a change in the direction of Iran for the common people, for the better good, and the direction that Iran may go down will be repetitive and a failure in some way or shape. Two: Despite the kindness that can be offered to Iran, there is no hope, and to the people when kindness is projected, they can't tell what it truly is due to the dehumanising nature of growing up in a household without rest from arduous chores. There is so much to pick out from a Kiarostami film, I love this with every word more I write of this, and I have also been reading a book on Iranian Cinema to gain more insight after adoring A Separation. A really highly-rated film for me, technically poignant, where a blend of an audience may believe it is an innocent film, or some may highlight the absurdity of all this trouble to give a notebook to complete homework, or the underlying damage that can cause kindness where everyone is blind to how the world works, that Iran expect the world to immediately be affectionate to them. Of course, I have a general understanding of Iran and a good understanding on the means of what makes a film brilliant, probably the longest review I done as it is so metaphoric and there is so much you can nit-pick on the basis of it being a film of a kid finding his friends house to return a notebook. The constant repetition of dialogue, the rooster's cries, the baby's screams, the same static extreme long-shots on Ahmed's journey to Poshteh, really makes this film feel like an experience, a feat accomplished by the wonderful Mr Kiarostami to heighten tension and suspense through constant, deliberate and annoying repetition of the basic means of sound. Damn. What a film. Is actually incredible what film can mean, and after only two A-level film lessons deep after GCSE, I feel I can write for days, as Kiarostami can seeminglessly make small stories feel with enormous, poignant weight.

"Mom, I accidentally took Mohammad Reza's book. I need to give it back." - Ahmed Ahmadpour And with something as simple as that, Ahmed, a boy from Koker, takes us on a journey to a distant neighbouring village called Postheh to return his friend's book before he gets expelled from class tomorrow morning for not completing his homework. The premise is simple, yet Abbas Kiarostami transformed it into a cinematic masterpiece. This is his most narratively conventional, but he still manages to fill each frame with the same humanism he displays throughout his oeuvre. Sometimes cinema doesn't need some gigantic tragedy to make us feel something. Sometimes all it needs is a boy trying to return his friend's notebook. And maybe that's why I have such a huge soft spot for this film. It feels strangely close to home, as I grew up in a similar mentality where children should be seen, not heard. Adults speak, and children do nothing but obey. Questions become disrespect, while disagreement becomes disobedience. And what makes the film even more interesting is how that behaviour becomes cyclical. Adults can reproduce the same dismissiveness and harsh discipline they themselves grew up with, passing it from one generation to another until nobody even remembers why children are supposed to obey in the first place. Here, Ahmed isn't fighting some grand villain. He's fighting a world of adults who simply won't fucking listen. That's what makes his tiny mission feel enormous. Again and again, we see expectations imposed on children by disciplinarians whose own behaviour can be contradictory. And through Ahmed's eyes, Kiarostami makes us understand how enormous these seemingly ordinary interactions can feel when you're young. Visually, Kiarostami once again applies his signature zig-zag road motif to symbolise his character's journey and life choices. Something as ordinary as a path across a hill can turn into an entire visual language. Ahmed doesn't simply travel from one village to another. He chooses to take that road. Not once, but twice. He could obey. He could forget about Mohammad Reza. He could decide that his friend's punishment isn't his responsibility. Instead, he keeps going. And that's what makes this tiny act so beautiful: he chooses empathy even when the adult world makes empathy inconvenient. There's so much more buried underneath that simplicity, too. Even questions of individual freedom and obligation toward others. Which eventually leaves me with a much larger question: how tf am I supposed to pursue my own freedom while preventing my neighbour from pursuing his? Suddenly, returning a notebook doesn't feel so small anymore. That's the magic of this film. Kiarostami takes an ordinary childhood problem and quietly expands it until you're thinking about society itself. What a marvellous film. I know I'll return to this one—not merely as cinema, but as a reminder of how we listen to children, how families communicate, and how something as small as taking another person's problem seriously can become an act of love. Maybe that's what I'll remember most. In a world where the adults repeatedly fail to listen to Ahmed, he never stops listening to his heart:)

Children's mind operate with the monotropism of autistic people. They cannot process anything until desired task is complete, entirely void of worry for the stress they put on their caregivers. Their empathy toward one another is like knowing it firsthand, a sort of phantom pain. That stubborn focus reminds me of when I was forbidden countless times never to play football in the house because i might break something. But how could I stop when I hadn't yet found the satisfaction of hitting a volley like that legendary Zidane volley against Leverkusen? The opportunity came when it was just me and my sister left in the house, turning the patio leading into the dining room into the ultimate pitch. I told her to cross the ball for me to catch on the volley and score through the living room. We did it about eleven or twelve times before she got fed up with doing the exact same thing without better results. On her very last attempt, I caught the ball clean, and it flew straight through the window. Yes, what I did was stupid, but i got the exact satisfaction i had been yearning for. I knew I was going to sleep with a swollen body from my grandfather's leather belt, so I dressed heavy like a medieval knight to cushion the blows. Interestingly enough, my sister never ratted me out, and I was never scolded for breaking the window, which felt very odd, because my grandfather would beat me for the pettiest things like breaking his cigarettes. Was the experiment worth it? Yell Yeah!!

"I'd find an excuse and give him a beating every other week. So he wouldn't forget." there’s something about kiarostami’s films that feels like a breath of fresh air. they have this incredibly rare ability to make me feel completely calm, almost as if the world slows down while i’m watching them. his stories are usually small-scale and slice of life, but that’s exactly what makes them feel so natural, he finds so much meaning in simply watching people exist and that becomes incredibly engaging. the children’s performances are especially incredible, there’s such a natural awkwardness to them but also so much subtle emotion in the way they react to adults, fear, and responsibility. i also love how much the film quietly says about childhood and the adults surrounding it. the parents are constantly occupied with their own concerns, while the children are left to navigate problems that feel enormous to them completely on their own. school is treated with frightening importance, and the fear of punishment hangs over everything they do. the notebook became more than just a notebook because returning it meant protecting his friend from a system that demands obedience without really caring about the individual children and their emotions. the conversation between the grandfather and elder especially reveals that. when one of them suggests that the other should find a reason to discipline the child, it becomes clear that punishment is not necessarily about what the boy has actually done, it is about maintaining authority and fulfilling an expectation. the child must be disciplined because that is what adults are supposed to do, even if there is no real logic behind it. that scene says so much about generational trauma and the way harmful systems continue through tradition. even the mother, she is so overwhelmed by domestic responsibilities and adult concerns that she has little time to understand what the child is actually going through. her attention is focused on keeping the household functioning, while the boy’s fear is treated as something small or inconvenient. the film shows how children can be neglected emotionally without anyone consciously deciding to neglect them. the adults’ behavior also reveals how easily people follow systems for the sake of following them. authority and social expectations seems to matter more than the actual circumstances of the child. the zigzag hill is probably the most memorable visual element for me. that winding path feels like a physical representation of the boy’s journey, constantly forcing him to go back and forth as he tries to find the right house. i also loved how distinct the different towns and landscapes felt, the houses and dirt paths gave the film such a strong sense of place. my favorite scene is probably the conversation with the old man near the end. there’s something so quietly beautiful about listening to him talk about how things have changed over time. after spending the entire film following this child through such a seemingly urgent problem, the conversation suddenly opens the film up to something much larger. generations pass, places change, people disappear, and yet the little moments of life continue. at the same time, the conversation connects back to the film’s ideas about inheritance because not only do people pass down memories and traditions, they also pass down fears, rules and ways of treating one another. kiarostami makes ordinary life feel meaningful without forcing it to be and there’s so much patience and humanity in his filmmaking. beneath that calm there is a sharp critique of the systems adults accept without question and the ways those systems shape children.
